- [USER] User provided a detailed paragraph discussing the findings of a study on social media effects on adolescents' well-being.
- [FACT] The study found that most adolescents do not experience short-term changes in well-being related to social media use.
- [FACT] The study indicated that when changes do occur, they are more often positive than negative.
- [FACT] The study suggests that small subsets of adolescents experience small to moderate changes in well-being.
- [FACT] The study highlights that overall effect sizes may mask individual differences in susceptibility to media effects.
- [FACT] The study confirmed that while overall effect sizes are small, person-specific effect sizes vary considerably.
- [FACT] The study disentangled associations of active and passive social media use.
- [FACT] Research among young adults found that passive social media use is associated with lower levels of affective well-being.
- [FACT] The current study showed that passive use of Instagram and WhatsApp seemed to enhance adolescents' well-being.
- [FACT] The study noted that adolescents often seek positive content on social media, such as humorous posts or memes.
- [FACT] The study found that time spent passively using WhatsApp improved adolescents' well-being uniformly.
- [FACT] The associations of time spent passively using Instagram with well-being differed among adolescents.
- [FACT] WhatsApp is described as a more private platform used for one-to-one communication.
- [FACT] Instagram is described as a more public platform allowing users to follow a diverse set of people.
- [FACT] The study revealed that the effect of social media use on well-being differs from adolescent to adolescent.
- [FACT] Participants in the study felt relatively happy overall.
- [FACT] The study suggests that more vulnerable samples may elicit different patterns of effects.
- [FACT] The study focused on affective well-being operationalized as happiness.
- [FACT] Future research should identify which adolescents are particularly susceptible to declines in well-being.
- [FACT] The study recommends including follow-up measures to understand the longer-term influence of social media on well-being.
- [FACT] The study suggests that research is needed to explore the unique effects of passive public use and passive private use of social media.
